items.explanation: The 1904 Corollary declared the U.S. an 'international police power' that could intervene in Latin America to keep Europeans out, prop up order, and remove unfriendly regimes — all three purposes at once.
options: A. Keeping European powers out of the Western Hemisphere
B. 'Assisting' Latin states in economic or political crisis
C. Removing hostile governments in the hemisphere
D. All of the above
items.stem: The Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine was intended

option_explanations.A: Keeping European powers out of the Western Hemisphere was the original Monroe Doctrine (1823) and part of the Corollary, but the Corollary went further — it claimed an American right to intervene directly. This alone understates what the Corollary was intended to do.
option_explanations.B: 'Assisting' Latin states in crisis — collecting debts, restoring order — was exactly the policing power Roosevelt claimed in 1904, but it was only one piece of the Corollary's purpose.
option_explanations.C: Removing hostile governments was indeed part of how the Corollary was applied, but again only one piece. The Corollary claimed all of these purposes at once.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The 1904 Roosevelt Corollary declared the United States an 'international police power' in the Western Hemisphere — empowered to keep Europeans out, intervene in Latin states' crises to preserve order, and remove unfriendly regimes. All three purposes were claimed together.

items.explanation: Spain's reconcentration camps in Cuba — herding civilians into disease-ridden camps to starve the insurgency — horrified American humanitarians and fed war fever in 1898.
options: A. They were horrified by Spain's reconcentration policy in Cuba
B. They ignored the yellow press's editorials
C. They wanted to help Filipino natives
D. They sought American economic interests in Cuba
items.stem: Many American humanitarians first backed the Spanish-American War because

option_explanations.A: Correct. Spain's 'reconcentration' policy — forcing Cuban civilians into disease-ridden camps to starve the insurgency — was widely reported in the American press, and the suffering it caused turned humanitarians toward war against Spain in 1898.
option_explanations.B: The opposite of what happened. The yellow press's lurid editorials about Cuban suffering fed the war fever; humanitarians absorbed that coverage rather than ignoring it.
option_explanations.C: American humanitarians in 1898 were focused on Cuba, not the Philippines. The war began over Cuba; the Philippine annexation debate — and the humanitarian outcry over subjugating Filipinos — came after the war.
option_explanations.D: Economic interests in Cuba motivated business-minded expansionists, not humanitarians. The humanitarians' argument was about Cuban suffering under Spain, not about sugar profits.

items.explanation: Roosevelt encouraged Panama's revolt against Colombia and then took the Canal Zone — a strong-arm land grab critics called unsavory even by imperial standards.
options: A. It would require two-ocean naval power
B. It would cost an outlandish sum
C. The U.S. used underhanded tactics to get the canal rights
D. It would require a permanent garrison in Panama
items.stem: Critics of the Panama Canal project chiefly objected that

option_explanations.A: Two-ocean naval power was an argument FOR the canal, not against it — Mahan and the imperialists wanted the canal precisely so the fleet could move between oceans.
option_explanations.B: The canal was enormously expensive, but cost was not the chief criticism leveled at Roosevelt's project — the moral objection was about how the United States got the rights in the first place.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Critics chiefly objected to the means: Roosevelt encouraged Panama's revolt against Colombia in 1903 and then took the Canal Zone — a strong-arm land grab that critics called unsavory even by imperial standards.
option_explanations.D: A permanent American presence in the Canal Zone did follow, but the chief contemporary objection was not to the garrison — it was to the underhanded way the rights were seized from Colombia.

items.explanation: American sugar planters, backed by U.S. marines, overthrew Queen Liliuokalani in 1893; annexation followed in 1898.
options: A. Queen Liliuokalani sought more American investment
B. Pro-American planters staged a revolt
C. Hawaiian public opinion demanded annexation
D. Hawaii feared other Pacific powers
items.stem: The United States was able to annex Hawaii because

option_explanations.A: Queen Liliuokalani opposed the American planters — she tried to restore native Hawaiian authority with a new constitution in 1893, which provoked her overthrow. She never sought more American investment as a path to annexation.
option_explanations.B: Correct. American sugar planters, backed by U.S. marines, overthrew Queen Liliuokalani in 1893; the republic they set up was annexed by the United States in 1898.
option_explanations.C: Native Hawaiian public opinion did not demand annexation — the overthrow was the work of a small planter minority, and the queen's supporters petitioned against annexation.
option_explanations.D: Fear of other Pacific powers was not the cause of annexation. The push came from American planters who wanted Hawaii inside the U.S. tariff wall, and they staged the revolt themselves.

items.explanation: Missionaries saw empire as a God-given field for evangelism — converting the 'heathens' of Cuba, Puerto Rico, and the Philippines.
options: A. They hoped to restrain other imperialists' zeal
B. They admired the spirituality of native peoples
C. European church leaders endorsed imperialism
D. They saw empire as a chance to convert new peoples
items.stem: American missionary leaders supported imperialism because

option_explanations.A: Missionaries did not oppose imperialism to restrain other imperialists — they actively supported American expansion because it opened new fields for their work.
option_explanations.B: Missionaries did not admire native spirituality; their purpose was to replace it. They supported imperialism as an evangelical opportunity, not out of respect for indigenous religions.
option_explanations.C: European church leaders' views were not the reason American missionaries backed imperialism. Their motivation was their own: empire meant new peoples to convert.
option_explanations.D: Correct. American missionary leaders supported imperialism because they saw empire as a God-given field for evangelism — a chance to convert the 'heathens' of newly acquired Cuba, Puerto Rico, and the Philippines.

items.explanation: Twain says it plainly: 'I have read carefully the treaty of Paris, and I have seen that we do not intend to free, but to subjugate the people of the Philippines.' The treaty's terms -- purchase of the islands from Spain with no provision for Filipino independence -- converted the former imperialist into vice president of the Anti-Imperialist League.
options: A. Reading the Treaty of Paris convinced him the U.S. meant to subjugate, not free, the Filipinos
B. He traveled to the Philippines and witnessed the war
C. He was offered a diplomatic post by the administration
D. He lost personal investments in Philippine ventures
items.stem: Twain describes himself as formerly 'a red-hot imperialist.' What changed his view?
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"I left these shores a red-hot imperialist. I wanted the American eagle to go screaming into the Pacific... But I have thought some more, since then, and I have seen that we do not intend to free, but to subjugate the people of the Philippines."
—Mark Twain, 1900 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: Correct. Twain says it in his own words: 'I have read carefully the treaty of Paris, and I have seen that we do not intend to free, but to subjugate the people of the Philippines.' The treaty's terms — the U.S. purchasing the islands from Spain with no provision for Filipino independence — is what changed his view.
option_explanations.B: Twain did not travel to the Philippines. His conversion came from reading the Treaty of Paris (1898) and seeing that it provided for subjugation, not liberation.
option_explanations.C: Twain was not offered a diplomatic post. He became vice president of the Anti-Imperialist League — the opposition, not the administration.
option_explanations.D: Twain lost no Philippine investments; his change of view was moral and political, driven by the treaty's terms, not by personal financial loss.

items.explanation: Twain and the Anti-Imperialist League argued that ruling the Filipinos without their consent betrayed the Declaration of Independence -- the old republican conviction, voiced since the founding, that empire abroad corrupts liberty at home. Annexation, they said, made America the very thing it had rebelled against in 1776.
options: A. The Federalist call for a strong navy
B. The republican fear that empire corrupts liberty at home
C. The Southern defense of slavery
D. The Whig program of internal improvements
items.stem: Twain's anti-imperialism most directly continues which earlier American tradition?
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"I left these shores a red-hot imperialist. I wanted the American eagle to go screaming into the Pacific... But I have thought some more, since then, and I have seen that we do not intend to free, but to subjugate the people of the Philippines."
—Mark Twain, 1900 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: The Federalists' call for a strong navy was about national defense, not about anti-imperialism. Twain's argument is about liberty, not naval power.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Twain and the Anti-Imperialist League argued that ruling the Filipinos without their consent betrayed the Declaration of Independence — the old republican conviction, voiced since the founding, that empire abroad corrupts liberty at home. Annexation, they said, made America the very thing it had rebelled against in 1776.
option_explanations.C: The Southern defense of slavery was a defense of bondage, the opposite of Twain's argument. Twain's tradition is the revolutionary one — government by consent — which the slavery defense rejected.
option_explanations.D: The Whig program of internal improvements was an economic program (roads, canals, banks), not a tradition of anti-imperialist thought. Twain's argument is political-philosophical, not economic.

items.explanation: Twain's indictment is moral, not fiscal or strategic: 'we do not intend to free, but to subjugate the people of the Philippines. We have gone there to conquer, not to redeem.' His objection is that annexation is conquest dressed as liberation -- a betrayal of the duty 'to make these people free.'
options: A. it would cost the United States too much money
B. it would provoke a war with Japan
C. it meant conquest and subjugation rather than liberation
D. it would grant Filipinos immediate American citizenship
items.stem: Twain's central objection to Philippine annexation was that it

"I left these shores a red-hot imperialist. I wanted the American eagle to go screaming into the Pacific... But I have thought some more, since then, and I have seen that we do not intend to free, but to subjugate the people of the Philippines."

option_explanations.A: Twain's objection was not fiscal. His indictment is moral — about subjugation versus liberation — not a complaint about what annexation would cost the Treasury.
option_explanations.B: Twain did not argue that annexation would provoke war with Japan. His objection was about what America was doing to the Filipinos, not about Pacific rivalries.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Twain's central objection: 'we do not intend to free, but to subjugate the people of the Philippines. We have gone there to conquer, not to redeem.' Annexation was conquest dressed as liberation — a betrayal of the duty to make the Filipinos free.
option_explanations.D: Twain never discussed granting Filipinos citizenship, immediate or otherwise. His objection was that the U.S. was subjugating a people rather than freeing them — not a debate about the terms of their incorporation.
